title: The Shroud Of Turin: No Ordinary Bed Sheet
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the Shroud of Turin, a roughly 3 by 4 foot herringbone linen cloth bearing the negative image of a crucified man, long venerated as Jesus's burial shroud. They cover its documented history from 1353 (Geoffrey de Charny) through Constantinople, Athens, France, and Turin; the 1898 photograph by Secondo Pia; the 1978 STURP scientific investigation; Walter McCrone's pigment claims; the 1988 carbon-14 dating that dated the cloth to 1260-1390 and the contamination and control-fabric debates; theories about how the image was made (bas-relief, scorching, Maillard reaction, piezonuclear fission, ultraviolet light); and 1990s DNA testing that found plant and human DNA from many regions. They conclude the mystery remains unsettled. Also includes an intro about Tripod month and a listener mail segment about an alarm clock clip.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

entities.name: Cathedral of St. John the Baptist

segments.title: Tripod month and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces Tripod month and encourages sharing podcasts. Josh and Chuck banter about infinity scarves and mention that Chuck was inspired by a William Friedkin interview on WTF with Marc Maron, in which Friedkin described seeing the Shroud in person and weeping.

segments.title: What the Shroud is and its religious significance
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Shroud as a roughly 3 by 4 foot herringbone linen cloth with a faint negative image of a bearded naked man with wounds consistent with crucifixion. They explain the believer view that it is Jesus's burial shroud, and note the Easter connection and the cloth's veneration.

segments.title: Shroud history: Constantinople, France, and Turin
segments.summary: The hosts trace the cloth's movement from Jerusalem to Constantinople, then Athens after the Crusades, then France, where Geoffrey de Charny documented it in 1353, and finally to Turin's Cathedral of St. John the Baptist. They note public display and the Catholic Church's changing official position.

segments.title: Secondo Pia's photograph and the negative image
segments.summary: Amateur photographer Secondo Pia photographed the Shroud, and the negative revealed a clearer human figure. Early accusations of forgery faded by the 1930s. Later image analysis suggests three-dimensional facial shape.

segments.title: STURP 1978 scientific investigation
segments.summary: In 1978, a team called STURP was granted five days of nearly continuous access to examine the Shroud. Its report said the image was not the product of an artist and that the stains tested positive for hemoglobin and serum albumin, though it was described as a mystery. The team included believers and skeptics, and the Vatican did not try to influence results.

segments.title: Walter McCrone's pigment claims and the blood debate
segments.summary: Microscopist Walter McCrone argued the marks are red ochre and vermilion pigment in a tempera binder rather than blood. Other researchers claimed blood, including blood type claims, and critics raised contamination and aging arguments. The hosts conclude the debate cannot be settled.

segments.title: Carbon-14 dating and the contamination debate
segments.summary: Labs at Oxford, University of Arizona, and ETH Zurich dated the cloth to between 1260 and the 1390s, long after Jesus's lifetime and near its first documented appearance. Critics argued contamination, patching, and fire damage affected results; the hosts note control samples matched their known ages and that the sample was taken from unpatched areas.

segments.title: How the image could have formed: theories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why the image is hard to replicate because the color penetrates only the outer fibers. They cover proposed explanations including bas-relief scorching, ultraviolet light, a Maillard reaction, dust transfer, and piezonuclear fission from an earthquake, noting each theory's problems.

segments.title: DNA testing results
segments.summary: DNA tests found human DNA from people in the Middle East, Europe, India, and Africa, plus plant DNA such as black locust, a rare Asian pear, and Mediterranean clover. The oldest DNA was from India, which some argue came from public display. The hosts say the DNA results added to the mystery rather than resolving it.

segments.title: Sources, sign-off, and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts recommend National Geographic and Live Science articles and Walter McCrone's site, then read a listener email from David and Jade about an alarm clock clip from the Action Figures episode, followed by social media and contact information.
